content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposes sequence generating BERT (BERT + SGM) and a mixed model for Multi-label text classification (MLTC). The mixed model is an ensemble of vanilla BERT and BERT+SGM models. The methods are examined on three MLTC datasets in either English or Russian. The mixed model has a 0.4%, 0.8%, and 1.6% improvement in hamming accuracy (HA), micro-F1, macro-F1, and accuracy compared with vanilla BERT.
 
Even though there are some accuracy improvements, it seems that most of the improvements are coming from the downstream task fine-tuning of BERT. Several questions and suggestions:
 
1. The mixed model seems to have a better performance on most of the datasets over original BERT on HA and micro F1, while it fails to compete with original BERT on macro F1. This may be a sign that the mixed model is overfitting and cannot generalize to an unbalanced dataset. 

2. Next, it would be great to add more math deductive reasoning and model analysis. Can you show the dramatic difference between BERT with one more layer and  BERT + SGM? In figure 1, it looks like we have an attention as a final “decision maker”, but does it make more correct decision compared with the normal BERT?

3. Furthermore, it would be better to have more convincing experiment results. The mixed model performs well around 0.45. Can you interpret with more reasoning or just intuitions? Or is it just a random threshold that we get for this downstream task?

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your valuable comments and suggestions. Our responses to your comments one by one are as follows:

1. As can be seen from results, in RCV1-v2 and Y.Riders datasets, BERT+SGM and the mixed model has a better performance in terms of maF1 if compared to original BERT. We can also see an improvement on Y.Drivers dataset for the mixed model comparing to vanilla BERT. These datasets are not seemingly different from the others in terms of class balance. However, it might be a good idea to check the results on more unbalanced datasets specifically.

2. One feed-forward layer is the baseline setup from the original BERT paper which is generally used to perform text classification. We would greatly appreciate if you could explain in a bit more details why do you think it would reasonable to compare the results to BERT with two feed-forward layers?

3. We are currently working on experiments and updating the results. The 0.4-0.45 threshold for obtaining BERT+SGM probability distribution vector can be treated as a fine-tuned hyper-parameter of the model. We will try to update the presentation of the work with more intuitive explanations and interpretations.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This is an empirical paper about the MLTC (Multi Label Text Classification) problem. They experiment on three different models. One method is the famous BERT model, which they use in the multi-label setting, by simply changing the activation function of the last layer of the original model to sigmoid. The second method, is BERT encoder combined with a Sequence Generation Model (SGM). For this one, they replace the encoder of a previous work (Yang et. Al.) with Bert encoder. And finally, the third model, is just an ensemble of the two previous mentioned methods: vanilla BERT and BERT+SGM.
Pros:
They have experimentally shown some improvements in the different MLTC metrics with (BERT+SGM) and mixed methods, compared to the vanilla BERT, specially, for data sets with hierarchically structured classes. 
They have shown better performance of (BERT+SGM) rather than BERT for training with 3-4 epochs, however with higher (20) epochs, BERT will eventually win!
Cons:
Their experimental improvement for their mixed method, is not as significant for public data sets, less than 1% on average.
They have reported 0.4%, 0.8%, and 1.6% average improvement in miF1, maF1, and accuracy measure for public data sets. I believe this is not exact. 
For example, the average set accuracy on public data sets is 0.8% instead of 1.6%. Or maF1 measure improvement on average is much less than 0.8%. For RCV1-v2 they have 0.55% improvement. But for the two other data sets they have lost 0.1% and 0.6% compared to the vanilla BERT. I am wondering how that comes to the average of 0.8% improvement on maF1 measure(?)
On one data set they have got 1.6% better accuracy but that is not on average, as how they have reported. 

I do not see much novelty in this work. They have combined two previous methods. Although it is always interesting to see that previous good methods can be combined to get better models, I expect a better performance improvement compared to the state-of-the-art methods for a paper that is empirically based.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer #3
content.comment:
Thank you for your review and valuable feedback! Below we would like to clarify some points from your questions.

Point 1. 
"For example, the average set accuracy on public data sets is 0.8% instead of 1.6%. Or maF1 measure improvement on average is much less than 0.8%. For RCV1-v2 they have 0.55% improvement. But for the two other data sets they have lost 0.1% and 0.6% compared to the vanilla BERT. I am wondering how that comes to the average of 0.8% improvement on maF1 measure(?)"

Response 1.
We’re sorry for this confusion, there was indeed a mix-up in the paper: “0.4%, 0.8%, and 1.6% average improvement in miF1, maF1, and accuracy” should actually be  “0.4%, 1.6%, and 0.8% average improvement in miF1, maF1, and accuracy”. Apart from that, everything else seems to be correct. For maF1 in RCV1-v2 dataset, the improvement is not exactly 0.55%, but (0.611 - 0.556) * 100% = 5.5%. Then the average is (5.5% - 0.1% - 0.6%) / 3 = 1.6%. We should also note, that 0.1% drop in the first dataset was not statistically significant, and in the other two datasets the maF1 metrics also improves.

Point 2.
"I do not see much novelty in this work. They have combined two previous methods. Although it is always interesting to see that previous good methods can be combined to get better models, I expect a better performance improvement compared to the state-of-the-art methods for a paper that is empirically based."

Response 2.
Currently, the sequence generation abilities of BERT is not a well-explored topic. Also, considering multi-label classification as sequence prediction task appears to be a new and promising view on this problem.

Pretrained language models such as BERT are current SOTA on text classification tasks, and sequence modeling is one of the effective approaches to use on multi-label text classification datasets according to recent works [1, 2]. We argue that we can improve the overall accuracy on MLTC datasets by bringing the best from both worlds. Current results show the proof of concept, but they indeed could be improved to be more convincing. We are currently working on experiments and updating the results.

As regards to the mixed model, combining two approaches in the form of mixing probabilities or target losses appears to be one of the working methods that helps to improve the results in hierarchical text classification [3, 4].

[1] Yuning Mao, Jingjing Tian, Jiawei Han, and Xiang Ren. Hierarchical text classification with reinforced label assignment. EMNLP 2019
[2] Jinseok Nam, Eneldo Loza Menc’ia, Hyunwoo J. Kim, and Johannes Fürnkranz. Maximizing subset accuracy with recurrent neural networks in multi-label classification. NeurIPS 2017
[3] Jonatas Wehrmann, Ricardo Cerri, and Rodrigo C. Barros. Hierarchical multi-label classification networks. ICML 2018
[4] Hao Peng, Jianxin Li, Yu He, Yaopeng Liu, Mengjiao Bao, Lihong Wang, Yangqiu Song, and Qiang Yang. Large-scale hierarchical text classification with recursively regularized deep graph-cnn. WWW 2018

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
The paper presents a method for multi-label text classification as a sequence generation task and using Bert model as an encoder. The paper shows that some improvement is obtained over methods on a collection of public and private datasets.
The paper's overall contribution and imapct seems quite limited. More concretely, some of the concerns regarding the paper are the following :
1. The proposed method of using Bert as an encoder does not appear really novel as it has been proposed in other works such as XBert [1] and to datasets at a much bigger scale.
2. The improvements over other methods is very little (around 0.5%) which can also be result of hyper-parameter tuning among other reasons.
3. The authors should evaluate their method on much larger scale datasets in multi-label classification and also compare with other state of the art methods such as those available from Extreme multi-label classification repository [2].

[1] XBert : X-BERT: eXtreme Multi-label Text Classification with BERT
https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.02331v2
[2] http://manikvarma.org/downloads/XC/XMLRepository.html

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer #1
content.comment:
Thank you for your review and your time! We have responded to each comment separately below:

1. The paper [1] on XBert that you mention seems to be largely different from the models we propose. In [1], the authors exploited BERT in combination with Deep Neural Matching and Ensemble Ranking, solving HMC problem. In our work, we use BERT encoder for label sequence generating and then propose a mixed model for solving multi-label and hierarchical text classification tasks. It appears that there are neither sequence modelling nor model mixing components in XBert, and the experiments performed on [1] are for another task and on other datasets.

2. On public datasets the average absolute improvement is around 0.9% and the relative improvement is 1.7% on average (0.5%, 2.9%, 1.8% for miF1, maF1, accuracy respectively). Also, in hierarchical datasets, the improvement is more visible.
Regarding hyper-parameters, for vanilla BERT model in text classification, there are general tips for tuning hyper-parameters and the set of common values of hyper-parameters is also known. For sequence generating BERT model, the number of hyper-parameters is larger, and it’s harder to optimize them. In our experiments, we did not perform thorough tuning of all hyper-parameters. We are currently working on experiments and updating the results.

3. The problem of extreme multi-label text classification is indeed outside the scope of this paper. We agree that it would be interesting to see the results on classification datasets with a larger scale. However, in this work, we focused on the classic multi-label and hierarchical text classification tasks and datasets following the recent works [2, 3, 4, 5].

[1] Wei-Cheng Chang, Hsiang-Fu Yu, Kai Zhong, Yiming Yang, Inderjit Dhillon. A Modular Deep Learning Approach for Extreme Multi-label Text Classification. https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.02331v2
[2] Yuning Mao, Jingjing Tian, Jiawei Han, and Xiang Ren. Hierarchical text classification with reinforced label assignment. EMNLP 2019
[3] Jinseok Nam, Eneldo Loza Menc’ia, Hyunwoo J. Kim, and Johannes Fürnkranz. Maximizing subset accuracy with recurrent neural networks in multi-label classification. NeurIPS 2017
[4] Jonatas Wehrmann, Ricardo Cerri, and Rodrigo C. Barros. Hierarchical multi-label classification networks. ICML 2018
[5] Pengcheng Yang, Xu Sun, Wei Li, Shuming Ma, Wei Wu, and Houfeng Wang. SGM: sequence generation model for multi-label classification. COLING 2018
